name: Moai
info: The moai are monolithic human figures carved from stone by the Rapa Nui people on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in eastern Polynesia, mostly between 1250 and 1500, and chiefly regarded as the living faces of deified ancestors.

facts.made: The Rapa Nui, the Polynesian inhabitants of the island, carving mostly between 1250 and 1500; oral tradition points either to a class of professional carvers or to members of each clan
facts.form: Monolithic figures with oversized heads and no visible legs, mostly of volcanic tuff from Rano Raraku, averaging about 4 metres in height and about 12.5 tonnes; the tallest erected, Paro, was almost 10 metres and 82 tonnes
facts.where: Rapa Nui, where nearly half remain at the Rano Raraku quarry and hundreds stand or lie on ahu platforms around the coast; ten or more were removed, including those now in the Louvre and the British Museum
facts.known: enormous heads with elongated noses and ears; red scoria topknots (pukao); coral and obsidian eyes; the quarry at Rano Raraku; the debate over how the statues were moved; their toppling; Hoa Hakananai'a in the British Museum

t: More than 900 statues were carved, mostly from the tuff of Rano Raraku, where 394 in varying states of completion are still visible; hundreds were moved to ahu platforms around the island's edge.

The Rapa Nui regarded the moai chiefly as the living faces of deified ancestors, and archaeologists suggest they were also symbols of religious and political authority charged with sacred spirit, or mana.

Every erected statue had fallen by the late 19th century, and about 50 have since been re-erected; the island's population was devastated by slave raids in 1862, and the site was listed by UNESCO in 1995.
dyk: The statues had eyes: in 1979 Sergio Rapu Haoa and a team of archaeologists reassembled fragments of white coral and showed that the eye sockets held coral eyes with black obsidian or red scoria pupils.

sections.origins:
The moai (moꞌai, "statue" in Rapa Nui) were carved by the Polynesian people of Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, in eastern Polynesia, mostly between 1250 and 1500. Their minimalist style reflects forms found throughout Polynesia, and the Polynesian ceremonial sites called marae are the places from which the moai and ahu traditions likely evolved. Pollen and charcoal in the sediment of the island's three main crater lakes suggest that the forests that originally covered the island were gradually logged between 800 and 1200 CE, while it was being settled by migrants from eastern Polynesia, and again in the decades or centuries before 1700.

The Rapa Nui regarded the moai chiefly as the living faces (aringa ora) of deified ancestors. Once erected on stone platforms called ahu, they may also have been regarded as the embodiment of powerful living or former chiefs and as lineage status symbols: the larger the statue placed upon an ahu, the more mana the chief who commissioned it was held to have. Mana was, in ancient Polynesian religions, a magical spiritual essence with which properly fashioned carved objects were believed to be charged.
sections.content:
The moai are whole-body statues, though popular writing often calls them "Easter Island heads", partly because the head makes up three-eighths of the figure and partly because the best-known photographs show statues on the slopes of Rano Raraku buried to the shoulders. The heads have heavy brows, elongated noses with a curl of the nostrils shaped like a fish hook, thin protruding lips and elongated oblong ears. The arms are carved in low relief and rest against the body, with long fingers along the hips and meeting at the loincloth (hami). Except for one kneeling moai, the statues have no clearly visible legs. The backs are generally not detailed, but may bear a ring and girdle motif on the buttocks and lower back.

The more recent moai wore a pukao, a cylinder of red scoria from a quarry at Puna Pau that represented the topknot of a chieftain; local tradition held that the mana was preserved in the hair, and red is a sacred colour in Polynesia. At least some statues were painted, and the eyes were of coral with obsidian or scoria pupils. Most ahu stand along the coast and face inland towards the community. The seven moai of Ahu Akivi face out to sea; a legend tells of seven men who waited for their king to arrive. Small wooden figures, the moꞌai kavakava, moꞌai paepae and moꞌai taŋata, were also carved.
sections.making:
The human figure was outlined on the rock wall of the quarry and chipped away until only the image was left. All but 53 of the more than 900 known moai were carved from the tuff, a compressed volcanic ash, of Rano Raraku; 13 are of basalt, 22 of trachyte and 17 of fragile red scoria. At the end of carving the builders rubbed the statue with pumice. Which groups carved the statues is not known exactly. Oral traditions suggest either a distinguished class of professional carvers comparable to the craft guilds of other Polynesian societies, or members of each clan; they also show that the quarry was divided into territories for each clan.

The quarries appear to have been abandoned abruptly, leaving stone tools, many completed moai awaiting transport and almost as many unfinished ones as were installed on ahu. One unfinished figure, had it been completed, would have stood about 21 metres tall and weighed about 145 to 165 tonnes. It is now generally believed that some statues were rock carvings never meant to be completed, that carvers abandoned a figure when they met hard inclusions in the soft tuff, that some finished statues were placed at the quarry permanently, and that some were unfinished when the statue-building era ended. A 2019 study concluded that quarrying may have been linked to improving soil fertility.
sections.reception:
How the statues were moved has been debated for a long time, since the island was largely treeless when Europeans arrived. Earlier researchers assumed ropes, wooden sledges or rollers and levelled tracks, and one estimate held that laying a statue on a sledge would have needed about 1,500 people for the largest erected moai. In 1998 Jo Anne Van Tilburg suggested that fewer than half that number could do it with a sledge on lubricated rollers; in 1999 she supervised a moai replica of nine tonnes, towed by 60 people, which moved on its second attempt once tracks were embedded in the ground. Oral histories tell that a king named Tuu Ku Ihu moved the statues with the help of the god Makemake, and later stories tell of a woman living alone on the mountain who ordered them about.

Scholars now largely support the view that the moai were "walked" upright with ropes. In 1986 Pavel Pavel, Thor Heyerdahl and the Kon-Tiki Museum walked a five-tonne and a nine-tonne moai, though the experiment ended early because the bases were chipped, and other scholars concluded for that reason that this was probably not the method. Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo, working with the Rapa Nui archaeologist Sergio Rapu, argue that the statues' wide, curved bases and forward lean made them rock sideways and take a step, and that statues fallen along the roads were those the teams could not keep upright. The debate continues.
sections.survival:
All of the moai erected on ahu were toppled in the years after Jacob Roggeveen's arrival in 1722. Some last standing statues were reported in 1838 by Abel Aubert du Petit-Thouars, but none remained by 1868, apart from the partly buried ones on the outer slopes of Rano Raraku. The toppling is attributed possibly to European contact or to internecine tribal wars. Oral histories include a clan pushing down a single moai in the night, others tell of the earth shaking, and there are indications that at least some fell in earthquakes. Some fell forward with their faces hidden and their necks broken; others fell off the back of their platforms.

The Rapa Nui people were devastated by slave traders who raided the island in 1862; within a year those who remained were sick or injured and lacking leadership. Missionaries converted the survivors to Christianity, their tattoos and body paint were banned, and they were made to live on a much smaller part of the island while Peruvians used the rest for farming. Ten or more moai have been removed to locations around the world, including the Louvre and the British Museum. Hoa Hakananai'a, decorated with maroon and white paint until 1868, when it was removed from the island, is in the British Museum, and demands have been made for its return to Rapa Nui. Cast replicas stand in several other museums.
sections.legacy:
The Routledge expedition of 1914 established a cultural link between the designs on the statues' backs and the island's traditional tattooing. Until modern DNA analysis of the islanders and their ancestors, this was key scientific evidence that the moai had been carved by the Rapa Nui and not by a separate group from South America. In the 19th century the abandoned quarries had led to the conjecture that the island was the remnant of a sunken continent with most completed moai under the sea; that idea has long been debunked.

From 1955 to 1978 the American archaeologist William Mulloy investigated the production, transport and erection of the statues and restored several ahu, among them Ahu Akivi, Tahai and the ceremonial village at Orongo. The Rapa Nui National Park and the moai were listed by UNESCO in 1995. The Easter Island Statue Project has documented many moai on the island and the pieces held in overseas museums, giving the results to the Rapa Nui families and the public agencies responsible for conservation. Today about 50 moai have been re-erected on their ahu or in museums elsewhere, and statues are still being discovered.

summary: The moai are the monolithic statues carved by the Rapa Nui on Easter Island, mostly between 1250 and 1500, chiefly as the living faces of deified ancestors. More than 900 were made, nearly half still at the Rano Raraku quarry; all the erected ones had fallen by the 19th century, and about 50 have been re-erected.
notes: Start 1250 with circa true: the article says carved 'between the years 1250 and 1500' and 'mostly between 1250 and 1500'.

How the moai were moved is disputed; the text reports the competing experiments and attributes each. The article also states that the toppling happened 'in the late 18th and early 19th centuries' and also 'in years after 1722'; the text follows the History section.

The article says the statues 'were toppled in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, possibly as a result of European contact or internecine tribal wars' but also lists earthquakes in oral histories; both are given.

Left out: the birdman cult (the article's account is thin and conflicts in tone with 'construction stopped'), moai kavakava being made 'after the civilization began to collapse', tourism incidents (2008 ear chip, 2020 truck, 2022 wildfire damage), emoji meme use. The moai kavakava claim was unhedged and left out; the 2022 fire damage could be added by the editor if wanted.

Article contradiction: average height about 4 m and 12.5 tonnes versus the tallest and heaviest erected; both given as stated. 'Nearly half still at Rano Raraku' (lead) vs 394 of more than 900 (description): consistent.
The article's Transportation section gives the 1,500-person estimate for laying a moai prone on a sledge without naming who estimated it.
The Heyerdahl 100 m a day estimate and Charles Love's experiments were left out for length.
